pairs.en: *“O marvellous wonder!* *The Fountain of life is laid in a tomb, and the tomb becomes a ladder to heaven.”* [Sticheron of the Dormition]

sections.heading: Wonderful in life and in death

pairs.en: The marvellous Mother of a marvellous God is marvellous from her beginning to her end, beloved listeners!
Marvellous in her life, and marvellous in her passing. The whole of her is one marvellous wonder!
Marvellous in her life, for she is a virgin Mother and a mothering Virgin, who bore God and yet did not break her virginity.
Marvellous also in her passing, for by her tomb she ascends not into the earth but into heaven, and “the tomb becomes a ladder to heaven.”

O marvellous wonder! The dead one is marvellous, and the tomb is marvellous! The dead one is alive even after death — “a Virgin in giving birth, and alive after death” — and the tomb reaches heaven, like that ladder of Jacob, set firm on the earth, whose top reached the heavens. The tomb is a ladder to heaven.

Let us take our stand, then, firmly with our mind beside this marvellous, deathless tomb of the deathless Mother of God, as beside a ladder leading up to heaven, and let us look closely with our inner eyes: what are the rungs of this ladder? For there is no such thing as a ladder without rungs. What are the rungs by which the Mother of God, at the hour of her passing, went up to heaven?

“O marvellous wonder! The Fountain of life is laid in a tomb, and the tomb becomes a ladder to heaven!” It would be no great wonder merely to stop up a fountain with a tomb, so that it no longer poured out its stream. The wonder is that the tomb is turned into a ladder — and a ladder reaching to the heavens. But can a human coffin, three cubits long, standing upright on the earth, at the same time reach the height of heaven?

Let it be known that here the word “tomb” is used in place of the word “death”: death is called a tomb, and also a ladder. For as a coffin is measured at three cubits, so is death. *“The death of his saints is precious before the Lord”* [cf. Psalm 115:6]: like a ladder raising the souls of the saints to heaven, it is measured by the three theological virtues — faith, hope and love. Great and high is this measure, reaching the heavens like a ladder! For faith reaches to the vision of God; hope reaches to the receiving of those good things *“which eye has not seen”* [1 Corinthians 2:9]; and love reaches to the very heart of God, which is the fountain and beginning of all love.

Death is a ladder. For as a ladder has two rails, two sides, so death — which ends this temporal life and begins eternal life — has, as it were, two rails, two sides, standing between the temporal and the eternal life: on the one side the life that is ending, on the other the life that is beginning. And as between the two rails the rungs for climbing are set and made fast, so at the time of death, between the life being ended and the life being begun, as between two rails, all the good deeds of a righteous man done in this temporal life are gathered together, and by them, as by rungs, the soul climbs up. Thus death, or the tomb, serves as a ladder for ascent: “The tomb becomes a ladder to heaven.”

sections.heading: Who has fallen asleep? The Handmaid of the Lord

pairs.en: The Mother of God ends her days with a most blessed ending; she dies a deathless death. On one side stands the end of her temporal life, on the other the beginning of life eternal. And in between, all her virtues have gathered and drawn themselves up, as rungs for the ascent of her most holy soul. Who can count them? Who can number and point out how, by what good deeds and how many, the Most Holy Virgin pleased God her Creator, from her youth to her most blessed end? It would be easier to count the flowers in spring, the ears of grain in summer, the fruits in autumn, the snows in winter! You will sooner count the hairs on a head, the drops in the sea, the stars in the sky, than number the good deeds of the Mother of God's pleasing of God, and her dignities! For my part, passing over all the rest, which is beyond counting, I shall consider only three most excellent things in her, which I take to be, as it were, the rungs of the ladder; and so that they may be seen more clearly, I shall put a question.

I will ask you: who is it that has fallen asleep? I know that each of you, according to his devotion to her who has departed, will answer with every kind of word of praise. One will say: “The Mother of God has passed over to her Son and God”; another will say: “The animate Heaven ascends into the heavens”; a third: “The impassable Gate has been carried to the doors of heaven”; another will say: “The Sun in which the Most High made his dwelling has gone up from earth to heaven”; another: “The most pure and most honourable House of God has been carried into temples not made with hands.” Each will say something in praise, according to his devotion. But I, turning to this most marvellous, immortal Dead One herself, ask: Who are you, lying here? And in answer I hear a humble voice: *“Behold, I am the Handmaid of the Lord!”* [Luke 1:38] Now let everyone know who has fallen asleep here: the Handmaid of the Lord has fallen asleep; the Handmaid of the Lord has been laid in the tomb: “Behold, I am the Handmaid of the Lord!” Here I will recall an ancient saying: “To serve God and to reign are one and the same” — that is, to serve God is at the same time to reign. The true servant of God is at the same time an heir of the heavenly kingdom; he reigns together with Christ. And if the Most Pure Virgin is the Handmaid of the Lord, then she must in truth be called also the Queen of all creation, visible and invisible.

But as I gaze attentively with my mind upon the Lord and upon his Handmaid, I see both my Lord, One in Three Persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — and his Handmaid, our Queen, who in her single person displayed three distinct forms of service to God: for in one special way she served God the Father, in another God the Son, and in another God the Holy Spirit. To God the Father she was a Daughter, to whom he says: *“Listen, O Daughter, and behold.”* [Psalm 44:11] To God the Son, a Mother; to God the Holy Spirit, a Virgin unwedded, a Bride unbrided. She served God the Father as a Daughter, God the Son as a Mother, God the Holy Spirit as a Virgin betrothed to him. She laboured for the Holy Trinity in these special ways, faithfully and truly.

Here I will ask again: by what rungs did this Handmaid of the Lord, who earned for herself royal honour, attain so great a dignity, so high an honour — to be Daughter of God the Father, Mother of God the Son, and betrothed Virgin of God the Holy Spirit? Truly she *“set ascents in her heart”* [Psalm 83:3]: she set in her life the rungs of ascent to God — namely, to her betrothal to God the Holy Spirit she climbed by virginal purity; to her motherhood of God the Son, by humility: *“He has looked,”* she says, *“upon the humility of his handmaid”* [Luke 1:48]; and she became Daughter to God the Father by love. And by those same rungs by which she drew near to God, One in Trinity, in her temporal life, she also went up, in her deathless Dormition, to heaven — to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit — that is, by virginal purity, by humility and by love.

First of all, from her youth she went up to God the Holy Spirit by virginal purity, becoming his living church and his animate temple. For nowhere does the Holy Spirit make his dwelling as he does in those who keep virginity, because virginity, by the testimony of the holy fathers, is kin to the Angels and friend to God. And the Most Pure Mother of God, in the words of St Ambrose, was a Virgin not only in body but also in spirit. Let us attend with our mind to the words of this teacher, who says of the Most Pure Virgin: “She was a Virgin not in body only, but also in spirit” — and let us consider: what does it mean to be virgin in body and in spirit? What does it mean to be pure in body and in spirit? And since we have brought up the subject of purity, let these words be heard not only by those who keep virginity, or the widowed, or those who guard their purity by repentance, but also by those living in marriage; for the apostle speaks to all without exception: *“Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you; you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you”*; and again: *“If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will punish him.”* [1 Corinthians 6:19; 3:16–17]

sections.heading: Purity for every state of life

pairs.en: So then, everyone must guard his own purity: the virgin his virginal purity, the widowed their widowed purity. In just the same way, those living in marriage must keep their conjugal purity blameless, so as to be pure temples of the Holy Spirit. For before God, as the purity of the unmarried is praiseworthy, so the purity of the married is honourable (“let marriage be held in honour among all” — Hebrews 13:4): the one is pleasing to him, and the other is not rejected, being undefiled; the one is glorious, and the other has its own glory too, though a different one, as the apostle says: *“There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, another of the stars.”* [1 Corinthians 15:41] Different, yes — but glory all the same, and to each its own: a special glory for the sun, a special one for the moon, and a special one for the stars.

St Isidore of Pelusium gives these apostolic words this interpretation: “Paul likens to the sun,” he says, “those who have loved to keep virginity; to the moon, those who abide in purity in their widowhood; and to the stars he likens those who in honourable marriage keep their bed undefiled. For as it befits the sun to be bright, and the moon to be bright, and the stars not to be dark, so it befits the virgin, the widowed and the married alike to be pure, that all may be worthy temples of the Holy Spirit.” Learn here, then, all of you, what it means for a person to be pure in spirit and in body.

sections.heading: Clean in body and clean in spirit

pairs.en: Every human being is by his very make-up twofold: outer and inner — that is, material and spiritual. The outer man is visible, being material; the inner is invisible, being spiritual. And therefore his purity too must be doubly blameless before God: purity of body and spiritual purity, that is, purity of spirit. In vain does a man pride himself in his mind on bodily purity if he does not carefully guard the purity of his spirit. In vain does he bridle his fleshly desires with abstinence if in his mind he nurses sinful filth. In vain does the outer man count himself clean if his inner man is being soiled with countless impurities. The body is clean — but out of the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, which defile a man. Such a person is like an apple of Sodom.

It is written in books that in the country where Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities were destroyed by the righteous wrath of God, there grow apples very beautiful in outward appearance, large, and of a marvellous colour. Anyone seeing them for the first time would be greatly struck by their beauty and would expect to find in them an indescribable taste. But when someone takes such an apple and cuts it open or bites into it, he finds in it nothing but rotten dust — stinking and noxious.

O man, clean in body and defiled in soul! Are you not like just such an apple? Is not the purity of your body like that apple, beautiful to look at, while the impurity of your spirit and mind is the rotten dust, stinking and ruinous to the soul? It is exactly such people that Christ the Lord himself, in the Gospel, likens to whitewashed tombs full of stinking bones [see Matthew 23:27], and says to them: *“You present yourselves as righteous before men, but God knows your hearts.”* [Luke 16:15]

Oh, if only one could look inside a heart that appears holy — more than one rotted and stinking corpse would be found there: a depraved thought! So it must be understood that the purity of the outer man, that is, purity of body, without the purity of the inner man, that is, of the spirit, is no purity at all. St Euthymius the Great explains it this way: “Let everyone know that even if a man does not touch another's body and commits no foul sin with his body, yet commits fornication in his mind — harbouring foul thoughts, holding on to them, submitting to them and taking delight in them — he is a fornicator and cannot be a temple of the Holy Spirit.” For the Holy Spirit, in St Chrysostom's phrase, is like a bee: “As a bee will not fly into a foul-smelling vessel, so the Holy Spirit will not enter an impure soul.” [Homily 15 on Ephesians 4:35]

But let us return to the words St Ambrose spoke about the Most Pure Virgin. She, he says, was a Virgin not in body only, but also in spirit. She was a Virgin in body, keeping the flower of her purity incorrupt; and she was a Virgin in spirit, never once thinking of marriage. For when, living in the Holy of Holies, she reached marriageable age, and the high priests and priests, following the lawful custom, directed her to leave her dwelling in the temple and, after the example of the other maidens of her years, to marry, she answered: “I was given by my parents from childhood to God alone, and I have vowed to keep my virginity for ever; therefore I cannot be joined in marriage to a mortal man, and nothing can compel me to marriage — me, a Virgin of the Immortal God.” Hearing this, the high priests marvelled at so unheard-of a thing, for never yet had there been a single maiden who had promised her virginity to God for ever; she was the first.

Who will not marvel that in all the time from Adam's transgression to the incarnation of the Word of God, who came to earth for the salvation of the human race in the middle of the sixth millennium, there was not found on earth one single virgin who was pure not only in body but also in spirit? She alone proved to be the first and the last such Virgin, who by her purity of body and soul was made worthy to be a church and temple of the Holy Spirit. And as then, through her virginal purity, she went up and drew near to God the Holy Spirit and was united into one spirit with God — as Scripture says, *“He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with the Lord”* [1 Corinthians 6:17] — so also in her most honourable Dormition, by that same rung she went up to heaven, into the heavens and above the heavens.

She went up to God the Son by the rung of humility, for through humility she was made worthy to be his Mother. By that same rung she also went up to heaven and surpassed in honour and dignity all the choirs of the saints. Humility is the best rung both to high earthly, worldly honours and to heavenly ones.

Once the forefather of the Theotokos and of Christ, holy David, being pursued by his father-in-law Saul, saw him at a distance in a certain place and cried out to him: “After whom do you go, and whom are you chasing? A dead dog, or a single flea?” And Saul, persuaded of his innocence and meekness, answered him: *“Now I know that you shall surely reign, and the kingdom of Israel shall be firm in your hand.”* [1 Kingdoms 24:15, 21] Look: when David humbled himself so far as to liken himself to a dead dog and a little flea, at once he heard the royal title God had prepared for him: “You shall reign.” Through humility he attained royal honour — earthly honours.

St John the Forerunner humbled himself down to the feet and the sandals of Christ, saying: *“I am not worthy to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandals.”* [Mark 1:7] And what did he hear from Christ? *“Among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist.”* [Matthew 11:11] By the rung of humility St John rose to so high a dignity that he was counted worthy to lay his hand upon the most honoured head of the Son of God.
But to the loftiest heavenly honours also there is no better ascent, no better rung, than humility, according to the Lord's words: *“He who humbles himself will be exalted.”* [Matthew 23:12]

Once a dispute arose among the apostles as to which of them was highest in the apostolic company, and who would hold command in heaven. They came to the Lord himself for the resolution of this question and said to him: *“Who is greater in the kingdom of heaven?”* *And the Lord, calling a child, set him in the midst of them and said: “Truly I say to you: unless you turn and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”* [Matthew 18:1–3]

But, O Lord! What does this teaching of yours mean? Must your disciples really turn from grown men into little children? Peter is already old, and Andrew too, and the other apostles are no longer young. Is it possible for them to go back to an age long past and become little boys again? Yet the Lord says: “Become children, if you wish to enter the kingdom of heaven and to be great in it.”

But, O Lord! Show us the way to turn back to childhood. The Lord says: *“Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greater in the kingdom of heaven.”* [Matthew 18:4] Here is the way of becoming a child: even in old age, to be humble, meek, guileless, like children. The apostle too speaks well of this: *“Do not be children in your minds: in evil be infants.”* [1 Corinthians 14:20] To him who is an infant in guilelessness and humility, the door of heaven is opened for his entrance; he will enter the heavenly kingdom and be great in it.

Such a turning back to childhood was necessary for Christ's disciples, because in their pride they had begun, little by little, to exalt themselves in their own minds: now they ask to sit at Christ's right hand and his left in his kingdom, now they argue over which of them is greater, seeking command. But no such turning back was needed for the Most Holy Virgin, for from her infancy she was unchanging in her humility; as she grew in body, she descended in the spirit of humility, and she was always child-like — like a little child in guilelessness and humility. She grew in years, and she grew in understanding, while with her God-contemplating mind she reached to heaven. She grew also in the height of her dignity, for she already knew that she, and no other virgin, was to bear the Son of God — which had been revealed to her by God the Father himself during her midnight prayer in the Holy of Holies. For a divine light shone upon her, and she heard the voice of God the Father saying: “You shall bear my Son.” How great an honour, how great a dignity!

And at such a height, does she think of any command, of sitting on a throne, of power? No! She is child-like in a child's humility, saying: “Behold, the Handmaid of the Lord!” It is as if she said: “I am unworthy not only to be, but even to be called, the Mother of the Lord my Creator; unworthy not only to reign with him, but even to stand before him; unworthy not only to carry him in my womb or in my arms, but even to look upon his most holy face, upon which even the Seraphim dare not gaze. Let me be but one of the maidservants who serve him: Behold, the Handmaid of the Lord.” O depth of humility! A depth “hard to gaze upon even for the eyes of angels!”

By this same high rung of deepest humility she attained the most exalted honour of bearing God, of incorrupt motherhood; for at the very time of her humble words — “Behold, the Handmaid of the Lord” — in her most pure virginal womb *“the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”* [John 1:14]

Humility is the foundation of everything, and all the other virtues serve, as it were, as the building raised on this foundation. And in her life the Most Pure Virgin drew near to God above all by humility — to God who says: *“To whom will I look, but to the meek and humble.”* [Isaiah 66:2] By that same humility, in her Dormition also, she went up into the heavens and was raised with glory onto the throne of the heavenly kingdom; for humility reigns with the Most Pure Virgin there, whence pride was cast down.

To the Third Person named, the Principal Person of the Holy Trinity, God the Father, she went up by a third and loftiest rung — love; for according to the apostle, *“love is the greatest of all.”* [1 Corinthians 13:13] Through love she became the Daughter of the Heavenly Father. How the Most Pure Virgin loved God, no tongue can express and no mind can grasp, for love is one of the unknowable secrets of the heart, known to God alone, *“who searches hearts and inward parts.”* [see Psalm 7:10] Yet in part even we can come to understand her love from certain outward actions, occasions and times — such as the following.

When the Child Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem, the Most Pure Virgin, on finding him, said: *“With great sorrow we have been searching for you”* [Luke 2:48] — that is, they searched with pain in the heart. Here we may say that the Most Pure Virgin loved God with all her heart. She stands by the Cross, watching the voluntary sufferings of her Son, and Simeon's words are fulfilled in her: *“And a sword shall pierce through your own soul also.”* [Luke 2:35] Here we may say that the Most Pure Virgin loved God with all her soul.

After the Lord's ascension into heaven the Most Pure Virgin remained on earth in the first Church, unceasingly keeping her Son and God in her thoughts, and constantly longing to depart from earth to him. Here we might say that she loved God with all her mind. And yet we shall never grasp, never adequately express, how she loved him with all her heart, with all her soul and with all her mind.

Reasoning in a human way, we might say that the Most Pure Virgin loved God as any of us loves his parents, or the companion who has become one flesh with him in marriage [see Ephesians 5:31], or his only sons. But among human beings the love of the heart differs according to its kinds: one loves a parent in one way, a friend in another, a son in another. The love of the Most Pure Virgin, however, knew no such distinctions, for the One whom she loved was for her at once Father, and only Son, and Incorruptible Bridegroom. The whole of her all-embracing love was directed towards the One God; and because of it she is called both Bride of the Holy Spirit, and Mother of God the Son, and Daughter of God the Father. And Daughter not by that adoption by which all become faithful children of God, according to the words of Scripture: *“To those who believe in his name he gave power to become children of God”* [John 1:12], and in another place: *“I will receive you, and I will be a Father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty”* [2 Corinthians 6:17–18] — no, the Most Pure Virgin became the Daughter of God the Father by another appropriation, incomparably higher, more honourable and closer.

Imagine that a certain man took in two little orphaned girls, brought them up as daughters and called them both his daughters, and then made one of them the bride of his own natural son. That girl, joined to his son, becomes by the law of nature his closest daughter, related to him in a higher degree than the girl who was not joined to his son. For the latter is his daughter only by outward adoption, only in name; but the former becomes his daughter by the law of nature as well, since she touches his nature — being joined to his natural son, she becomes one flesh with him, and thus, like the son, by the law of nature she is made a daughter of that same father. In just the same way we must understand the Most Pure Theotokos.

God the Father took to himself our human nature, and in particular the Most Pure Virgin, as it were two orphaned girls, as daughters. Our nature was orphaned, for it had lost paradise and the original grace of God. The Most Pure Virgin too was orphaned, having lost her parents. The Lord named our nature his daughter: *“You shall be,”* he said, *“my sons and daughters.”* He named the Most Pure Virgin his Daughter as well, saying: *“Listen, O Daughter, and behold, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father's house.”* [Psalm 44:11] And when the fore-appointed time came, God the Father joined the Virgin to his Son, the Word, as a Bride; and so the Most Pure Virgin became a closer Daughter to God the Father, joined to him far more nearly than we are, for she touched the nature of God, being united to God the Word by her own flesh, in which she gave him flesh within herself. And therefore the Virgin Mary is the Daughter of God the Father who is nearer to him than the whole of human and angelic nature. Moreover her motherhood too, since she bore God the Son, clearly shows her greater nearness to God the Father. That is why God the Father says to her in the Song of Songs: *“I have likened you to one near to me”* [Song of Songs 1:8]; for as he begot his own natural God the Son without a mother, so she bore that same God the Son — not another — without a father, and became, as it were, a closest Sister in relation to God the Father.

This dignity, so very great, the Most Pure Virgin attained both by the virtues already spoken of — virginity and humility — and by love. For the Lord says: *“I love those who love me.”* [Proverbs 8:17] And as the Most Pure Virgin loved God with a warmer love than the saints past, present and future, so God loved her more than all; he made her his own, joined her closer than all, entrusting to her the carrying in a virginal womb, and the bearing, of perfect God in perfect humanity. And as then the Most Pure Virgin went up by the rung of love to so high a nearness to God the Father, so now, in her most honourable Dormition, by that same rung she has gone up to heaven.

So by these three rungs (I say nothing of the countless others) the Mother of God goes up today into the heavens: to God the Holy Spirit by virginal purity, to God the Son by humility, and to God the Father by love. I will say more: by all these rungs together she went up to the One God in Trinity. For that by which she pleased God the Holy Spirit, by the same she pleased God the Son and God the Father also. That by which she pleased God the Son, by the same she pleased God the Father and God the Holy Spirit. That by which she pleased God the Father, by the same she pleased God the Son and God the Holy Spirit.
And we, marvelling at such an ascent of hers, at these rungs, let us cry out with trembling: “O marvellous wonder! The tomb becomes a ladder to heaven.” Amen.
